cards.text: Chronicles opened with Adam and walked us down through the nations (1 Chronicles 1). Now it reaches the twelve sons of Israel, the name God gave Jacob (Genesis 32:28): Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Joseph, Benjamin and six more. TWELVE boys, friend, and I needed a nap after raising six cookie cutters.

cards.question: Out of all twelve sons of Israel, whose family does the list zoom in on first?

cards.text: Judah's first three sons are born to him by Bath-shua the Canaanite: Er, Onan and Shelah. Er is the firstborn, and the list stops right here to tell us how the LORD sees him.

cards.question: Er, Judah's firstborn, was ___ in the sight of the LORD.
Because Er was wicked in the sight of the LORD, the LORD put him to death.

cards.text: Then two more sons come along for Judah: Perez and Zerah. Their mother is NOT Bath-shua, and this family tree just got complicated.

cards.question: Who is the mother of Judah's sons Perez and Zerah?
Counting Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez and Zerah, Judah had five sons in all.

cards.text: Perez has two sons, Hezron and Hamul, and Zerah has five. Next in the list is Carmi's son Achar, who brought trouble on Israel by violating the ban on devoted things, and every family's got that one name that makes the whole room go quiet.
Hezron has three sons: Jerahmeel, Ram and Caleb. Hold onto Ram like the last cookie in the box, because his son Amminadab is the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon gets a title next to his name.

cards.question: Nahshon, son of Amminadab, was a ___ of the descendants of Judah.

cards.text: Nahshon's son is Salmon. And Salmon's son is a name you might know from the book of Ruth, a man with a big field and a BIGGER heart (Ruth 2:3).

cards.question: Who is Salmon's son, the man from the book of Ruth?

cards.text: Boaz is the father of Obed, and Obed's son will be the father of a shepherd boy who becomes king (1 Samuel 16:11-13; 2 Samuel 5:3). Friend, we are getting CLOSE.

cards.question: Boaz's son Obed is the father of ___.

cards.text: Jesse's sons get listed oldest first: Eliab the firstborn, then Abinadab, then Shimea, and on down the line. It's like the family photo where somebody's aunt lines everybody up oldest to youngest and nobody's allowed to argue.

cards.question: Who comes seventh, last in the list of Jesse's sons?

cards.text: Those seven brothers have two sisters, Zeruiah and Abigail. And their boys are about to sound VERY familiar.

cards.question: David's sister Zeruiah is the mother of Joab, the man who later commands David's army (2 Samuel 8:16).
David's sister Abigail is the mother of ___, whose father was Jether the Ishmaelite.

cards.text: Then the list circles back to Hezron's other sons, Caleb and Jerahmeel: wives, sons, clans, even fathers of towns, like Salma the father of Bethlehem. Two standouts: Caleb's great-grandson Bezalel, the craftsman God filled with skill to build the tabernacle (Exodus 31:2-7), and Sheshan, who has only daughters, gives one in marriage to his Egyptian servant Jarha, and their line runs on for generations. Thirty-eight verses of names, friend. I've stamped fewer cookies on a holiday weekend.
Now the list lands on David's own sons born in Hebron. The firstborn is Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel, and the second is Daniel, by Abigail of Carmel.

cards.question: All six of David's sons born in Hebron have the same mother.
Absalom, David's third son, is the son of Maacah, and her father is a king. Who is he?

cards.text: David reigns in Hebron seven years and six months. Then he reigns in Jerusalem, and he's there a LOT longer.

cards.question: How long does David reign in Jerusalem?

cards.text: In Jerusalem, four sons are born to David by Bathsheba daughter of Ammiel. And one of those four is a name EVERYBODY knows.

cards.question: Which son of David is one of Bathsheba's four?

cards.text: Then nine MORE sons, not counting the sons by his concubines, and two of them are named Eliphelet. TWO, friend, and I bet calling those boys in from outside got confusing real quick.

cards.question: After all of David's sons, the list names one sister: ___.

cards.text: Now the list follows Solomon's line, son after son. Solomon's son is Rehoboam, then Abijah, then Asa, then Jehoshaphat, handed down like Grandpa's old watch.

cards.question: From Solomon on down the list, each name is the son of the one before him.
The run of names, father to son, from Solomon ends with ___.

cards.text: Josiah has four sons: Johanan, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah and Shallum. Then Jehoiakim's son Jeconiah gets one word next to his name, and friend, that one word tells you a LOT about him.

cards.question: The list calls Jehoiakim's son Jeconiah the ___.

cards.text: Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim was carried away to Babylon (Jeremiah 24:1). But the names keep right on coming: Shealtiel his son, then Malchiram, Pedaiah and more.

cards.question: Which son of Pedaiah has the same name as the governor of Judah in Haggai 1:1?

cards.text: From Zerubbabel the list keeps rolling through his children and the lines of Hananiah, Shecaniah and Neariah, down to Elioenai's seven sons, and David's line is STILL going. Me, I gave up on myself for a while in that junk drawer, and this family tree just kept on GROWING.

findings.problem: The whole passage (1 Chronicles 2:1-3:24) is a genealogy. The walkthrough sums up 2:18-55 as one long-stretch card, but it puts choice cards on the rest, which are also name lists: 2:1-17, David's sons in 3:1-9, the king list in 3:10-14 and the post-exile line in 3:17-24. Under the long-stretch rule, none of these name lists would get choice cards. That would leave the passage with almost nothing to ask about.
findings.question: When a whole passage is a long stretch, like a genealogy or a name list, how should Prep handle it? Should it be one summary card with no choice cards? Or can the moments the text pauses on (Er's death, Achar, Nahshon's title, Boaz, David as seventh son, Jeconiah the captive) be treated as standout details that get choice cards? And if so, how many stops and cards should it have?

findings.problem: Story card 2 has already named Amnon's mother (Ahinoam of Jezreel) and Daniel's mother (Abigail of Carmel). That shows the Hebron sons don't all share one mother, so the true-or-false answer is given away. The card also uses 'six' from 3:4 but cites 3:1-3.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: Story card 11 already says the list follows Solomon's line 'son after son,' so the true-or-false answer is given away.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: Story card 5 says David is in Jerusalem 'a LOT longer' than seven and a half years. That setup rules out the 'Twelve years' answer.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Story card 7 says one of Bathsheba's sons is 'a name EVERYBODY knows.' That rules out the obscure wrong answers Ibhar and Nepheg, so Solomon is the only possible pick.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Boaz is called 'a man with a big field' and cited to Ruth 2:3. That verse only says the field belonged to Boaz and never says it was big. The detail is presented as a cited fact, not as a joke.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: Many choice cards can only be answered by luck or by outside knowledge, not reasoned out from the earlier cards. Examples: stop 1 card 2 (which son comes first), card 4 (wicked or faithful or blameless, with no hint in card 3), card 19 (Joab's mother) and card 20 (Amasa); stop 2 card 4 (Talmai of Geshur), card 10 (Tamar), card 13 (where the run ends) and card 17 (needs Haggai). Together with the cards whose answers are given away, discovery questions make up most of the choice cards instead of just a few.

rule.text: A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: The closing joke sets Papa Dorin giving up in the drawer against the family tree growing. That is a contrast of opposite actions, not a comparison with the same action. It also lands as a heavy line rather than a laugh.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.
